ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry Consultation — Abraham Lincoln

text.paragraph: Moderate major depressive disorder, single episode, in a 32-year-old attorney starting sertraline 50 mg daily. Please confirm the diagnosis, look for bipolar spectrum illness, review his suicide risk and safety plan, and advise on medication management and psychotherapy. [S]
Urgency: Routine; booked for the day of his six-week review. No current suicidal ideation. [S]

list.item: Do you agree with the diagnosis of a single, moderate, uncomplicated episode of major depressive disorder, and is there any sign of bipolar spectrum illness or another condition that would change treatment?
Is sertraline 50 mg daily an appropriate first choice, and when should the dose be increased?
Please review his suicide risk and the collaborative safety plan.
Would you add psychotherapy, and how long should treatment continue after remission?

text.paragraph: Mr. Lincoln is seen at the request of Dr. Marquez six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg daily for a depressive episode with low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, and poor concentration. His mood is brighter on most days, he is back at court on his usual schedule, and he writes to friends again. He falls asleep within half an hour and wakes once a night. Mild nausea settled by the third week; he has had no restlessness, agitation, or sexual side effects, and he misses about one dose every two weeks. He describes no past periods of elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, racing thoughts, or unusual risk-taking, and no hallucinations or unusual beliefs. He uses no alcohol, tobacco, or other drugs. He has had no suicidal thoughts since the intake visit and carries his safety plan. No prior suicidal behavior is recorded. He lost his mother at nine and his older sister in his late teens, and he spoke about those losses without current preoccupation. He prefers to continue medication alone for now. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Abraham Lincoln was born February 12, 1809, near what is now Hodgenville, Kentucky. [D]
In 1859 Lincoln described himself as "six feet, four inches, nearly" in height. [D]
In his tenth year Lincoln was kicked by a horse and, in his own account, "apparently killed for a time." [D]
On January 23, 1841, Lincoln wrote to John T. Stuart, "I am now the most miserable man living." [D]
Lincoln’s recurrent melancholy is retrospectively interpreted by modern clinicians as chronic depression that did not prevent him from leading the nation. [R]
Lincoln’s mother, Nancy Hanks Lincoln, died of milk sickness on October 5, 1818, when he was nine. [D]

Marfan syndrome, or another inherited marfanoid disorder such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B, has been proposed retrospectively from Lincoln’s build; the diagnosis is disputed and has never been genetically confirmed. [R]
Lincoln’s older sister, Sarah Lincoln Grigsby, died on January 20, 1828, at age twenty-one, from complications during delivery that also took her infant’s life. [D]

list.item: Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate (F32.1). Diagnosis confirmed. The episode is uncomplicated: no psychotic features, no substance use, and no earlier episode on record. The PHQ-9 has fallen from 14 to 9 in six weeks, a 36 percent reduction: a partial response that is still improving on a well-tolerated starting dose. [S]

Bipolar spectrum illness. Not suspected. There is no history of hypomanic or manic symptoms and no activation on sertraline. No Mood Disorder Questionnaire was done at intake; after this interview it adds little now. [S]

Suicide risk. Acute risk is low: no ideation, intent, plan, or preparatory behavior; access to lethal means has been reviewed; he is engaged in care and has strong protective factors in his friendships and his sense of purpose. The active depressive episode keeps risk above his baseline until remission. The collaborative safety plan is appropriate, and outpatient care is the right setting. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: PHQ-9 14 at intake and 9 today; the intake safety assessment and collaborative safety plan; today's vital signs; the medication list. No laboratory tests are on record, and none are needed for sertraline. [S]

list.item: Continue sertraline 50 mg daily; he is improving steadily and tolerating it well. [S]
Increase to 100 mg if the PHQ-9 is not below 5 at the twelve-week review. [S]
PHQ-9 at least monthly until remission, so a nurse telephone check in about four weeks, then every two to four weeks in the continuation phase. [S]
Reassess suicide risk at every visit with the C-SSRS Since Last Visit or PHQ-9 item 9, and keep the safety plan current; 988 at any time. [S]
After remission, continue sertraline at the dose that achieved it for at least six months, then taper gradually with his clinician rather than stopping suddenly. [S]

Psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral or interpersonal therapy) is a reasonable addition but not required for an uncomplicated episode. He prefers medication alone, and the guideline supports monotherapy; offer it again if his response stalls or he relapses. [S]
No laboratory monitoring is needed for sertraline. Avoid regular NSAIDs and other serotonergic drugs such as tramadol, triptans, St John's wort, and dextromethorphan without checking first. [S]
Reassess for bipolar disorder, using the Mood Disorder Questionnaire, if elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, or racing thoughts appear. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Marquez in person today; the patient agrees with the plan. [S]

Follow-up: Primary care will continue measurement-based care on the CMID schedule. Psychiatry will see him again if the PHQ-9 has not halved after a dose increase, for any suicidal ideation, or for features of bipolar disorder. [S]
